slides.title: Purpose and method
bullets: The white-cell count gives general quantitative information and helps to detect bacterial, viral or parasitic infection.
Leukocytes are counted under the microscope in a counting chamber or on automatic/semi-automatic electronic counters.

In a Neubauer (or improved Neubauer) chamber it is recommended to count all leukocytes in the whole marked zone (9 mm²); many laboratories count about half of it. The Goryaev chamber was widely used in laboratories of the former USSR.
Red cells are lysed with an acetic acid solution, after which only the leukocytes are counted.

slides.title: Reagent and dilution
bullets: Acetic acid solution: 2% stained with methylene blue (0.38 mL) in the Aripova book, 3% (0.4 mL) in the QVP book; in both, the blood is diluted 1:20 (20 µL of blood).
Keep strictly to the concentration in the laboratory’s instructions: acetic acid above 5% also lyses the leukocytes and lowers the result.
A counting chamber and matching cover glass, stoppered tubes, a 20 µL pipette, a rubber bulb.
A microscope: 10× objective and 10× eyepiece.

slides.title: Procedure
bullets: 1. Pour the acetic acid solution into the tubes and label them with the requisition number.
2. Take 20 µL of capillary blood without bubbles, wipe the pipette outside, check the blood level.
3. Expel the blood into the acid tube (1:20) with a rubber bulb or an automatic pipette (never by mouth) and rinse the pipette three times in the solution.
4. Mix the contents thoroughly for at least a minute (stopper the tube and invert it).

slides.title: Procedure
bullets: 5. Rub the cover glass on until Newton’s rings appear; fill the chamber by touching its edge with the pipette — do not overfill.
6. Leave the chamber for the cells to settle (Aripova: 2 minutes; QVP: at least 1 minute).

slides.title: Counting and calculation
bullets: Count at low magnification (10× objective, 10× eyepiece) with weak light (condenser lowered, diaphragm closed down).
After the red cells are lysed, count the leukocytes in 100 large squares (1600 small ones) of the Goryaev grid.
Cells on the upper and left lines of each square are counted as well.
For the Goryaev chamber with 100 large squares and a 1:20 dilution: X = a × 50 (a = number of leukocytes counted).
Example (QVP): 100 leukocytes in 1600 small squares → 5000 cells/µL.
Range in the books: 4.0–10.0 × 10^9/L.

slides.title: Sources of error
bullets: Uneven distribution of cells in the chamber is the commonest source of error; the chamber is left to stand before counting and counting over the whole ruled area is advised.
A badly seated cover glass changes the chamber volume and gives a wrong result.
A wrong ratio of blood to acetic acid.
Acetic acid stronger than 5% also lyses the leukocytes and lowers the result.
Leaving the sample for a long time at a temperature above 28 °C.

slides.title: Quality control
bullets: For the counting-chamber method there is little control to compare against, so every step of the test and of standardisation is carried out carefully.
Stabilised blood, special suspensions, haemolysates and fixed smears are used as control materials.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Treat all specimens as potentially infectious; blood work is done in rubber gloves with a single-use scarifier.
Never draw material into a pipette by mouth; use a rubber bulb.
Do not use glassware with chipped edges.
